```{r}


keep <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10
dds <- dds[keep,] # around 10,000 rows removed


dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("BOR", "R", "NR"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)

res_df <- as.data.frame(res) |>
  rownames_to_column("gene") |>
  filter(gene != "") |>
  mutate(direction = case_when(
    !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange >  1 ~ "Up in R",
    !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "Up in NR",
    TRUE ~ "Not significant"))
table(res_df$direction)

top_label <- res_df |> filter(direction != "Not significant") |>
  arrange(padj) |> head(15)

ggplot(res_df |> filter(!is.na(padj)),
       aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), color = direction)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_text_repel(data = top_label, aes(label = gene), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Up in R" = "#d95f02", "Up in NR" = "#1b9e77",
                                "Not significant" = "grey75")) +
  labs(title = "Volcano plot: R vs NR", x = "log2 fold change (R vs NR)",
       y = "-log10 adjusted p-value", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9
top_genes <- res_df |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> arrange(padj) |> head(40) |> pull(gene)

mat <- t(scale(t(assay(vsd)[top_genes, ])))          # z-score per gene
annot <- data.frame(BOR = coldata$BOR, row.names = colnames(mat))

pheatmap(mat, annotation_col = annot, show_colnames = FALSE,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         main = "Top 40 DE genes (vst, row z-score)")
```

```{r}




# T6: Rank genes for GSEA -----------------------------------------------------------
## Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) needs a single ranking metric per
## gene rather than a significance cutoff. Extract the "stat" column from
## the DESeq2 results (the DESeq2 test statistic) and name the resulting
## vector with the gene IDs.
##
## Why might the "stat" column be a more suitable ranking metric for GSEA
## than log2FoldChange alone? Remove any missing values before continuing.

ranked_genes <- res$stat
names(ranked_genes) <- rownames(res)

## Remove missing values from the ranked gene list
ranked_genes <- ranked_genes[!is.na(ranked_genes)]


# T7: Run fgsea against MSigDB gene sets ---------------------------------------------
## Load the GO Biological Process gene sets (collection "C5", subcollection
## "BP") from MSigDB for human genes, and reshape them into the named-list
## format that fgsea expects (one character vector of gene symbols per
## pathway).
##
## Run fgsea() using these gene sets as pathways and your ranked gene list
## as the ranking statistic.

gene_sets <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "C5", subcollection = "BP") # molecular signature database
gene_sets <- split(x = gene_sets$gene_symbol, f = gene_sets$gs_name) # converts to a format needed by fgsea

set.seed(42) # reproducible permutations
fgsea_res <- fgsea(pathways = gene_sets,
                   stats = ranked_genes, # stats: gene names for GSEA
                   nPermSimple = 10000) # raise from the default 1000 to resolve more pathway p-values


# T8: Visualize the enriched pathways -------------------------------------------------
## a) Bar plot: take the top 5 pathways by adjusted p-value and plot their
##    normalized enrichment scores (NES).
##    What does a positive vs. a negative NES mean here?

topPathways <- fgsea_res  |>
  dplyr::arrange(padj) |>
  dplyr::slice(1:5)

ggplot(topPathways,
       mapping = aes(x = reorder(pathway, NES),
                     y = NES)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Pathway",
       y = "Normalized Enrichment Score (NES)",
       title = "Top 5 Enriched Pathways") +
  theme_minimal()

## b) GSEA table: select the top 10 up- and top 10 down-regulated pathways
##    by p-value, and use plotGseaTable() to visualize them together.
##    Save the plot to both a PDF and a PNG file.

number_of_top_pathways_up <- 10
number_of_top_pathways_down <- 10

topPathwaysUp <- fgsea_res[ES > 0][head(order(pval), n = number_of_top_pathways_up), pathway]

topPathwaysDown <- fgsea_res[ES < 0][head(order(pval), n = number_of_top_pathways_down), pathway]

topPathways <- c(topPathwaysUp, rev(topPathwaysDown))


pdf(file = "PMC_gsea_top_pathways.pdf", width = 20, height = 15)
plotGseaTable(gene_sets[topPathways], stats = ranked_genes, fgseaRes = fgsea_res, gseaParam = 0.5)
dev.off()

png("my_results_gsea_top10pathways.png", width = 20, height = 15, units = "in", res = 300)
plotGseaTable(gene_sets[topPathways], stats = ranked_genes, fgseaRes = fgsea_res, gseaParam = 0.5)
dev.off()

## c) Many enriched pathways overlap heavily in their gene content.
##    collapsePathways() reduces the results to a smaller set of more
##    independent "main" pathways. Use it, and list the main pathways
##    ordered by NES.

```

## RQ3 — Biomarker comparison (Giosuè)

How do PD-1 (PDCD1) expression, immune-related gene signatures, and tumor mutational burden (TMB) compare in their association with different treatment responses? Suggested tasks:

```{r}
library(immunedeconv)
library(ggplot2)
library(limma)
library(gridExtra)

data <- readRDS("/home/projects/22123/IMvigor210_plain.rds")
counts <- data[["counts"]]
tpm <- data[["tpm"]]
clinical <- data[["clinical"]]
```

```{r}
all(clinical$pat_id %in% colnames(counts))

# Reorder expression columns to match the phenotype table.
counts <- counts[, match(clinical$pat_id, colnames(counts)), drop = FALSE]

# Explicitly verify the resulting sample order.
stopifnot(identical(clinical$pat_id, colnames(counts)))

print(table(clinical$BOR, useNA = "ifany"))

# Tumor mutational burden
TMB <- clinical$TMB

# Extract PDCD1 expression.
"PDCD1" %in% rownames(counts)
PD1 <- as.numeric(counts["PDCD1", ])

GEP_genes <- c(
  "CD27", "CD274", "PDCD1", "CD276", "CD8A", "CMKLR1",
  "CXCL9", "CXCR6", "HLA-DQA1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E",
  "IDO1", "LAG3", "NKG7", "PDCD1LG2", "PSMB10", "STAT1", "TIGIT"
)

GEP_genes_present <- GEP_genes[GEP_genes %in% rownames(counts)]
GEP_genes_missing <- setdiff(GEP_genes, rownames(counts))

cat("GEP genes present:", length(GEP_genes_present), "of", length(GEP_genes), "\n")
# All 18 present

# Extract GEP genes.
GEP_counts <- counts[GEP_genes_present, , drop = FALSE]

# Standardize each gene across samples.
# scale() operates on columns, so transpose before and after scaling.
GEP_counts_scaled <- t(scale(t(GEP_counts)))

# Average standardized expression across GEP genes for each sample.
GEP_scores <- colMeans(GEP_counts_scaled, na.rm = TRUE)
```

• Perform appropriate statistical tests to investigate whether each biomarker differs significantly between response groups.

```{r}
plot_Response_boxplot <- function(data, variable, y_label, test_result) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = Response, y = .data[[variable]])) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5) +
    annotate(
      "text",
      x = Inf, y = Inf,
      label = paste0("p = ", signif(test_result$p.value, 3)),
      hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5
    ) +
    labs(
      x = "Response class",
      y = y_label
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  sample = clinical$pat_id,
  TMB = TMB,
  PD1 = PD1,
  GEP_scores = GEP_scores,
  Response = factor(clinical$BOR))

stopifnot(identical(df$sample, colnames(counts)))
```

```{r}

GEP_plot <- plot_Response_boxplot(df,
```

• Compare the direction and magnitude of the observed differences, and discuss which biomarkers show stronger associations with treatment response.

```{r}
TMB_Response_test <- wilcox.test(TMB ~ Response, data = df)
PD1_Response_test <- wilcox.test(PD1 ~ Response, data = df)
GEP_Response_test <- wilcox.test(GEP_scores ~ Response, data = df)

TMB_Response_test # W = 564.5, p-value = 1.73e-05
PD1_Response_test # W = 1211, p-value = 0.000721
GEP_Response_test # W = 1199, p-value = 0.0006106

aggregate(
  cbind(TMB, PD1, GEP_scores) ~ Response,
  data = df,
  median
)

kendall_results <- lapply(c("TMB", "PD1", "GEP_scores"), function(v) {
  test <- cor.test(
    df[[v]],
    as.numeric(df$Response == "R"),
    method = "kendall",
    exact = FALSE
  )

  data.frame(
    Biomarker = v,
    Kendall_tau = unname(test$estimate),
    p_value = test$p.value
  )
})

do.call(rbind, kendall_results)
```

Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to compare biomarker distributions between responders (R) and non-responders (NR). This non-parametric test is appropriate because the two response groups are independent, their sizes are unequal (25 responders and 167 non-responders), and it does not require the biomarker values to follow a normal distribution.

All three biomarkers showed statistically significant differences between response groups (p \< 0.001), with higher median values in responders. TMB increased from 7 in non-responders to 14 in responders, PDCD1 expression from 18 to 42, and the GEP score from -0.26 to 0.31.

Kendall's rank correlation was used to assess the direction and strength of the association between each biomarker and treatment response. This method is suitable because response is a binary variable (NR or R), and it does not assume a linear relationship or normally distributed biomarker values.

All three biomarkers showed statistically significant positive associations with treatment response. TMB had the highest correlation (τ = 0.30), while PDCD1 and GEP showed weaker associations (τ = 0.20 for both).

Despite statistical significance, the correlation coefficients indicate that all three associations are relatively weak, with TMB showing a modestly stronger association. Therefore, none of the biomarkers individually demonstrates a strong association with treatment response.

• Explain the biological information captured by each biomarker and discuss their relative strengths and limitations

**Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB)** measures the number of somatic mutations per megabase of tumor DNA. A higher TMB can increase the likelihood of generating neoantigens, which may be recognized by the immune system and trigger an anti-tumor response. Its main strength is that it provides an indication of the potential immunogenicity of a tumor; however, not all mutations generate immunogenic neoantigens, and TMB does not directly measure immune cell infiltration or activity.

**PDCD1 expression** measures the expression of the gene encoding PD-1, an immune checkpoint receptor primarily expressed on activated T cells that regulates immune responses. Its relevance is particularly important in the context of immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, as blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway can restore aspects of anti-tumor immunity. However, elevated PDCD1 expression alone cannot distinguish productive immune activation from dysfunctional or exhausted T cells.

**T-cell-inflamed Gene Expression Profile (GEP)** summarizes the expression of 18 immune-related genes involved in T-cell infiltration, cytotoxic activity, antigen presentation and interferon signalling. It therefore provides a broader representation of the immune state of the tumor microenvironment. Its main strength is that it captures multiple aspects of anti-tumor immunity rather than relying on a single gene. However, bulk gene expression cannot distinguish between different cell populations, and averaging standardized expression values may conceal differences between individual immune pathways.

Overall, the three biomarkers capture complementary aspects of tumor immunology: TMB reflects the potential for tumor antigen generation, PDCD1 reflects immune checkpoint activity, and GEP reflects the overall immune activity of the tumor microenvironment. Although TMB showed the strongest association with treatment response in our analysis, all three associations were relatively weak. Combining these biomarkers could therefore provide a more comprehensive characterization of tumor immunogenicity and immune activity than relying on any single biomarker.

## RQ4 — The influence of tumor purity on immune-related biomarkers (Zoja)

How might differences in tumor purity influence the expression of immune- related biomarkers and their observed associations with treatment response?

Suggested tasks:

• Discuss how tumor purity may influence PD-1 expression and T-cell–inflamed GEP scores measured using bulk RNA-seq.

• Consider whether differences in tumor purity could partly explain the associations observed in RQ2 and RQ3.

• Discuss whether adjusting for tumor purity would necessarily improve the interpretation of these biomarkers.

note: makesure the clinical rows follow the expression column order



```{r}
# Align clinicaldata and expression
clin <- clinical |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(sample_id %in% colnames(tpm)) |>
  mutate(BOR = factor(BOR, levels = c("NR", "R")))

log_tpm <- log2(as.matrix(tpm[, clin$sample_id]) + 1)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(log_tpm), clin$sample_id))

clin |> count(BOR)
```

```{r}
# Biomarkers on normalised expression
GEP_genes <- c("CD27", "CD274", "PDCD1", "CD276", "CD8A", "CMKLR1",
               "CXCL9", "CXCR6", "HLA-DQA1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E",
               "IDO1", "LAG3", "NKG7", "PDCD1LG2", "PSMB10", "STAT1", "TIGIT")

expr_long <- log_tpm |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "gene") |>
  filter(gene %in% GEP_genes) |>
  pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "expr")

stopifnot(n_distinct(expr_long$gene) == length(GEP_genes))

gep <- expr_long |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  mutate(z = (expr - mean(expr)) / sd(expr)) |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(GEP = mean(z))

pdcd1 <- expr_long |>
  filter(gene == "PDCD1") |>
  dplyr::select(sample_id, PDCD1 = expr)

# TMB is right-skewed: log2-transform it, as in Exercise 7.
# Rank-based tests (Wilcoxon, Spearman) are unaffected by this.
markers <- clin |>
  transmute(sample_id, BOR, TMB = log2(TMB + 1)) |>
  left_join(pdcd1, by = "sample_id") |>
  left_join(gep,   by = "sample_id")
```

### Estimate the tumor purity

Write what estimate does

```{r}
est <- log_tpm |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter_common_genes(id = "hgnc_symbol", tidy = FALSE,
                      tell_missing = TRUE, find_alias = TRUE) |>
  estimate_score(is_affymetrix = FALSE) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(purity = cos(0.6049872018 + 0.0001467884 * estimate))

est |> summarise(across(purity, list(min = min, median = median, max = max)))
# check: values should be within 0–1

# Join by sample ID, never by row order
dat <- markers |>
  left_join(est, by = c("sample_id" = "sample"))

stopifnot(!anyNA(dat$purity))
```

### biomarker-respose association with and without urity

- odds ration,likelihood ratio
```{r}
standardise <- \(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)

assoc <- function(m, adj) {
  d <- dat |>
    drop_na(all_of(c(m, adj))) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(c(m, adj)), standardise))

  fits <- list(
    crude    = glm(reformulate(m, "BOR"),         family = binomial, data = d),
    adjusted = glm(reformulate(c(m, adj), "BOR"), family = binomial, data = d)
  )
  base <- glm(reformulate(adj, "BOR"), family = binomial, data = d)

  lrt_p <- anova(base, fits$adjusted, test = "LRT") |>
    tidy() |>
    pull(p.value) |>
    dplyr::last()

  fits |>
    imap(\(fit, model) tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
           filter(term == m) |>
           mutate(model = model)) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(marker = m, adjusted_for = adj,
           n = nrow(d), n_R = sum(d$BOR == "R"), LRT_p = lrt_p)
}

assoc_long <- expand_grid(marker = c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB"),
                          adj    = c("purity", "stromal")) |>
  pmap(\(marker, adj) assoc(marker, adj)) |>
  list_rbind()

# Summary table: crude vs adjusted OR, % change in log-OR, LRT
assoc_tab <- assoc_long |>
  dplyr::select(marker, adjusted_for, n, n_R, model, estimate, LRT_p) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = estimate,
              names_prefix = "OR_") |>
  mutate(pct_change_logOR = 100 * (log(OR_adjusted) - log(OR_crude)) / log(OR_crude))

assoc_tab
```

```{r}
p_forest <- assoc_long |>
  mutate(model = if_else(model == "crude", "crude", str_c("adj. ", adjusted_for))) |>
  distinct(marker, model, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, marker, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio for response (per 1 SD, log scale)", y = NULL,
       colour = NULL, title = "Biomarker–response association") +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r}
resid_tab <- c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB") |>
  map(\(m) {
    d <- dat |> drop_na(all_of(m))
    d <- d |> mutate(resid = residuals(lm(reformulate("purity", m), data = d)))

    tibble(
      marker  = m,
      n       = nrow(d),
      n_R     = sum(d$BOR == "R"),
      p_raw   = wilcox.test(reformulate("BOR", m), data = d)$p.value,
      p_resid = wilcox.test(resid ~ BOR, data = d)$p.value
    )
  }) |>
  list_rbind()

resid_tab
```

### Visuals

Discussion points (claude for now\<3)

\- \*\*Why purity matters in bulk RNA-seq.\*\* Each sample is a mixture of cells. Lower purity means more immune and stromal RNA, so PDCD1 and the GEP partly measure \*how much non-tumour tissue was sampled\*, not only how inflamed the tumour is.

- \*\*Could purity explain the RQ2/RQ3 results?\*\* Only if purity differs between response groups \*and\* correlates with the marker. Section 1 and section 2 test those two conditions separately. A marker whose OR barely changes after adjustment is robust to purity.

\- \*\*TMB.\*\* TMB comes from DNA sequencing, not from RNA. Low purity lowers variant allele fractions, so it can make the measured TMB lower than the real one. TMB is affected through a different mechanism than the RNA markers.

\- \*\*Adjusting is not automatically better.\*\*

- ESTIMATE purity is computed partly \*from immune genes\*, so adjusting the GEP for it is circular and can remove exactly the T-cell signal that predicts response. This is over-adjustment. - Infiltration is part of the causal path: an inflamed tumour \*is\* a lower-purity tumour.

- Stroma also matters (Mariathasan: TGFβ-rich, T-cell-excluding stroma predicts non-response), so low purity can mean "inflamed" or "excluded". - ESTIMATE purity on RNA-seq is an approximation without a reference such as pathologist estimates or ABSOLUTE.

\- \*\*Better alternatives\*\* include deconvolution of cell fractions (e.g. CIBERSORTx, quanTIseq) and spatial phenotyping (inflamed / excluded / desert, as in the paper).
